Lighthouse keepers return to Gull Rock after forty years

By Marta Quillfeather

For the first time since the light was automated in 1986, people are living on Gull Rock again. A crew of six volunteers moved into the restored keepers' cottage last week, carrying their supplies up the 140 stone steps from the landing stage by hand.

The group, which calls itself the Gull Rock Light Society, spent three summers repairing the slate roof and replacing the rotten window frames. "We wanted the building to be lived in, not just looked at," said Ilse Brannock, who chairs the society. "A lighthouse without keepers is a beautiful machine, but it is only half of the story."

A rota of volunteers

The volunteers will stay in fortnightly shifts until the end of October. Each shift keeps a logbook of the weather, the passing ships and the seabirds nesting on the western cliffs, continuing a record that the last keepers stopped writing four decades ago.

Keepers on the first shift said the hardest part was the silence after dark, broken only by the turning of the lamp and the wind against the tower. Several of them had never spent a night without mains electricity or a phone signal.

The light still turns every ten seconds, exactly as it did when my grandfather wound the clockwork by hand.

That was how Tomas Elderberry, whose family kept the light for three generations, described his first evening on the rock. He brought his grandfather's brass oil can with him and placed it on the kitchen shelf where it used to stand.

What the restoration involved

The society's report lists the main works, which were paid for by a local appeal and a heritage grant of eighteen thousand pounds. The report also notes that the original iron railings were kept wherever the metal was still sound.

Visitors will be able to book day trips from the harbour from next spring, weather permitting. The society hopes that a permanent exhibition about the keepers' daily routine will open in the old oil store, using the logbooks, letters and photographs that families have lent to the project over the last three years.

Anyone who would like to join a future shift can apply through the society, which asks only that volunteers are able to climb the steps and are happy to share a small kitchen with five strangers.
